title: Good Practices, Debugging, Reproducibility
markdown: ## What this covers Every other unit in this course is about getting a computation to produce a correct number. This one is about something adjacent but different: making sure the code that produces the number can be read, trusted, fixed when it breaks, and rerun by someone else (including you, in six months). It answers three practical questions in turn — how should code be written so a person can safely change it, how do you find the point where it went wrong when it does, and what has to be true of a project for its results to be reproducible? The chapter assumes you can already write Python functions, loops and conditionals; nothing here depends on a specific algorithm from an earlier unit. ## Who is going to read your code Two audiences make these habits worth the effort: other people (a grader, a collaborator, a reviewer of your package), and future-you, who will not remember why a piece of code did what it did. The tips below split roughly into two kinds — some are aimed at software you intend to hand to others or maintain over time, some are aimed at a one-off analysis — and it is usually clear from context which applies. A good editor or IDE (VS Code, Emacs, Sublime, vim, or the editor built into an environment like RStudio) is worth using regardless: syntax colouring, automatic indentation, parenthesis matching, line numbers, and being able to run and debug code from inside the editor all reduce the number of bugs you introduce in the first place. ## Writing readable code The [PEP 8 style guide](https://peps.python.org/pep-0008) is the reference for Python style; the points below are a mix of PEP 8 and general habits. - **Header comments.** Put metadata — who, when, what the file does, how it fits into a larger program, the versions of Python and key packages you used — in the first few lines as comments. - **Docstrings** for public modules, classes, functions and methods; a short comment after the `def` line is enough for non-public ones. - **Indentation and whitespace.** Python enforces indentation, which is a feature: it forces symmetry that helps you (and others) see the structure of the code and exposes some bugs directly. Use 4 spaces, not tabs. Put whitespace around operators, between function arguments, and between list or array elements, even where it is not required for precedence — `a/y * x` is safer to read than `a/y*x`, because a slip in operator precedence is now visible rather than hidden in a run of characters. - **Line length**: code under about 79 characters, comments and docstrings under about 72. - **Comments** should be complete sentences and should explain the *why*, not restate the *what* (`x = x + 1 # increment x` teaches nothing). Worth documenting: what a block of code does, why a complicated expression (a gnarly regular expression, say) is doing what it's doing, and where an otherwise-mysterious constant comes from. - **Method chains** can be split across lines and commented piece by piece by wrapping the whole expression in parentheses: ```python newdf = ( pd.read_csv('file.csv') .rename(columns={'STATE': 'us_state'}) # adjust column names .dropna() # remove some rows ) ``` - **File size.** For software development, keep files to roughly 2000–3000 lines, with related functions grouped together and meaningful file names. - **Naming.** PEP 8's convention: `UpperCamelCase` for classes, `snake_case` for functions, methods and variables, and a leading underscore for anything non-public. Names should be informative but not padded, and functions should be named like verbs (`calc_loglik`, not `loglik` or `loglik_calc`) because a function *does* something. Don't shadow a built-in name like `len` — Python's namespace system will let you get away with it, which is exactly the problem. - Learn from other people's code, and expect other people to read yours: this semester, someone (the GSI, the instructor) reads your problem sets, which is as good a reason as any to practise these habits now. ## Structuring code for reuse A second layer of advice is less about how a single line looks and more about how a project is put together. - **Break tasks into core units** and keep a single copy of any piece of reusable logic — under version control — so that a change only has to be made once. - **Prefer functions to scripts that operate on specific named objects.** A function that takes data as an argument, rather than code that assumes a variable called `df` already exists in the environment, can be reused, tested in isolation, and re-run later without reading through the body to reconstruct what it depends on. This is also the first step toward reproducibility: an analysis built out of functions with explicit inputs and outputs can be rerun on new data or checked against old results. - **Functions should be modular** (one task each), have a meaningful name, and carry a docstring describing purpose, inputs and outputs. - **Don't hard-code numbers.** Even a genuine physical constant is better as a named variable — `speed_of_light = 3e8` — because it documents intent and makes the code easier to change and read. - **Practise defensive programming**: check function inputs and warn if the code will do something unexpected; check the condition passed to `if` (in Python, any expression other than `False`, `0`, `None`, or an empty list/tuple/string is treated as `True` there); give sensible default arguments; document the range of valid inputs; check that output is valid; and fail with an informative error message rather than silently continuing. The mechanics of doing this with exceptions and assertions are below. - Avoid code that depends on a specific operating system where you can help it. - Ask others to review your code, and review theirs — and be willing to rewrite code once you understand the actual shape of the problem, since analyses tend to meander away from whatever the code was originally organised around. ### Linting Linting applies a tool to your code to enforce style automatically, rather than by memory. `ruff` is one such tool (`black` is another); a typical session first checks for problems, then reformats: ```bash ruff check test.py ``` ``` All checks passed! ``` ```bash cp test.py test-save.py # so we can see what `ruff` did ruff format test.py ``` ``` 1 file reformatted ``` ```bash diff test-save.py test.py ``` ``` 1c1 < x= 7 --- > x = 7 3,5d2 < def myfun(x, y =0): < # This is a toy function. < return x*y 6a4,6 > def myfun(x, y=0): > # This is a toy function. > return x * y ``` `ruff` fixed the spacing around `=` and properly indented the comment — exactly the class of mechanical style issue that isn't worth policing by hand. ## Exceptions, assertions and testing These three tools are what make "defensive programming" concrete: together, they make it more likely that a bug produces a loud, informative failure close to its source, rather than a wrong number that surfaces much later. ### Exceptions A *syntax error* is invalid Python; an *exception* is code that is syntactically fine but fails at run time — a missing file, an unreachable URL, permission denied, an invalid input. You raise one yourself to tell the caller that a task failed, and why: ```python def myfun(val): if val <= 0: raise ValueError("`val` should be positive") myfun(-3) ``` ``` ValueError: `val` should be positive ``` Sometimes you want the opposite: to keep going even when something inside a loop fails. Wrap the risky call in `try`, and handle the failure in `except`: ```python for i in range(n): try: result[i] = except: result[i] = None ``` You can also let a function fail gracefully and return something useful instead of propagating the error: ```python import os def myfun(filename): try: with open(filename, "r") as file: text = file.read() except Exception as err: print(f"{err}\nCheck that the file `{filename}` can be found " f"in the current path: `{os.getcwd()}`.") return None return text.lower() myfun('missing_file.txt') ``` or catch an error just long enough to add context, and then re-raise it so execution still stops: ```python import requests def myfun(url): try: requests.get(url) except Exception as err: print(f"There was a problem accessing {url}. " f"Perhaps it doesn't exist or the URL has a typo?") raise myfun("http://missingurl_forsure.com") ``` ### Assertions An assertion is a quick way to raise `AssertionError`: a sanity check that a condition you believe should always hold actually does, mostly useful during development (and typically disabled for performance in production runs). A common use is checking preconditions and postconditions — a condition that should only fail if there is a bug. ```python number = -42 assert number > 0, f"number greater than 0 expected, got: {number}" ``` Common patterns: ```python assert x in y assert x not in y assert x is y assert x is not y assert isinstance(x, ) assert all(x) assert any(x) ``` Assertions are just as useful mid-pipeline in a data analysis — checking that a data frame has the expected shape, or that no values are missing or absurdly large, at various checkpoints. ### Testing Testing is what you already do informally after writing code, to check it works; for code that matters (functions others will call, or that you'll rely on for months), encode that checking so it survives you forgetting to do it by hand. Some people write the test suite *before* the code, partly because it forces you to think through the intended behaviour, including how the code should fail on bad input. *Unit tests* check individual functions, which is another reason to keep functions small and modular. The `pytest` package is the recommended tool: ```python import pytest import numpy as np import dummy def test_numeric(): assert dummy.add_one(3) == 4 def test_numpy_array(): assert np.all(np.equal(dummy.add_one(np.array([3,4])), np.array([4,5]))) def test_bad_input(): with pytest.raises(TypeError): dummy.add_one('hello') def test_warning(): with pytest.warns(UserWarning, match='complex'): dummy.add_one(1+3j) ``` Running `pytest` on this file reports which tests pass and prints a traceback for the ones that don't, e.g. a failure because `add_one` was only written to handle scalars: ``` test_dummy.py .F.. [100%] FAILED test_dummy.py::test_numpy_array - TypeError: `[3 4]` should be numeric 1 failed, 3 passed in 0.84s ``` `pytest` run with no arguments looks recursively for files with "test" in the name, so a whole suite can be run from the top of a project. *Continuous integration* (CI) is running that test suite automatically whenever the code changes, rather than trusting yourself to remember. The most common route is GitHub Actions: a YAML file in `.github/workflows` says when to run (on push, on pull request, ...), how to set up the environment, and what to run. GitHub then executes those steps on a fresh virtual machine (the *runner*), which also catches the common failure mode where tests pass on your machine and nowhere else: ```yaml on: push: branches: - main jobs: CI: runs-on: ubuntu-latest steps: - uses: actions/checkout@v4 - name: Set up Python uses: actions/setup-python@v5 with: python-version: 3.12 - name: Install mytoy and pytest run: | pip install pytest pip install --user . - name: Run tests run: | cd mytoy pytest ``` (Across languages the tools change but the idea doesn't: R's rough equivalents are the `assertthat` or `checkmate` packages for assertions and `testthat` for unit tests.) ## Version control, and AI-assisted coding tools Use version control — Git — even on a project only you will ever touch; it is the nearest thing to a time machine for code, and pairs naturally with an issue tracker (or at minimum a to-do file) and good commit messages. Git itself is covered in its own unit, not here. A newer addition to the toolbox is AI-assisted coding: tab-completion suggestions, chat/edit/agent panes built into an IDE (GitHub Copilot and Gemini Code Assist inside VS Code, or Cursor, which is built on VS Code), and the ability to hand a tool whole files or directories as context. This is a fast-moving area, but a rough hierarchy of trust is worth keeping in mind: lean on these tools freely for straightforward syntax you can check by eye (formatting a plot); use them more cautiously for small, testable pieces (a regular expression you'll verify against cases); and for anything resembling the actual analysis or algorithm, read and understand every line before it becomes part of your code. Generated code you don't understand is exactly the code most prone to a hidden bug and hardest for you to maintain later. ## Debugging ### Reading the traceback When an error occurs partway through a chain of nested function calls, Python prints the *call stack* — the sequence of calls that led to the error — as a *traceback*. Read it from the bottom, where the actual error message and the frame in which it fired are; that frame is often in a function you didn't write, in which case the bug is usually in the arguments *your* code supplied at the last frame you did write. Two general habits, before reaching for a debugger: - **Fix the first error, from the top down**, when a run produces a cascade of them — a long stream of errors is very often one root cause with a lot of noise downstream of it. - **Check whether the bug is reproducible.** If restarting Python changes the behaviour, suspect variable scoping: a global variable your code was silently relying on, present in the current session but not always. If the error message alone doesn't localise the problem, build the code up (or tear it back) in pieces, or use a binary-search strategy — halve the code, find which half the error is in, halve again — until the offending piece is isolated. Code that is already broken into small functions is easier to check this way, since you can test each function directly against its inputs and outputs. Print statements (the debugging strategy of the 1970s) still work and are sometimes the fastest option, and stepping through code line by line is reasonable for simple cases; but for errors buried in several layers of nested calls, in scoping issues, or inside functions you didn't write and can't step into, a real debugger is faster. ### Using `pdb` Python's built-in debugger is `pdb` (`ipdb` is a nicer wrapper for IPython/Jupyter; VS Code provides a graphical debugger with the same underlying commands). You can enter it in several ways: inserting `breakpoint()` at a location of interest, calling `pdb.pm()` after an exception to inspect the state at the point of failure, running a function under `pdb.run()`, or starting a whole script with `python -m pdb file.py`. **Stepping through with a breakpoint.** Suppose `run_with_break.py` fits a regression separately to each stratum of some data, with a `breakpoint()` inserted at the top of the loop: ```python import run_with_break as run run.fit(run.data, run.n_cats) ``` ``` >>> run.fit(data, n_cats) > .../run_with_break.py(10)fit() -> sub = data[data['cats'] == i] (Pdb) ``` `n` runs the current line and stops at the next one; `c` continues to the next time the breakpoint is hit (i.e. the next iteration of the loop); `p i` prints the current value of a variable: ``` (Pdb) n > .../run_with_break.py(11)fit() -> model = statsmodels.api.OLS(sub['y'], statsmodels.api.add_constant(sub['x'])) (Pdb) c > .../run_with_break.py(10)fit() -> sub = data[data['cats'] == i] (Pdb) p i 1 ``` Stepping through every iteration this way to find the one that fails would be tedious — which is what *post-mortem* debugging is for. **Post-mortem debugging.** Running the same computation without a `breakpoint()`, then calling `pdb.pm()` after it raises, drops you directly into the frame where the error occurred: ```python import pdb import run_no_break as run run.fit(run.data, run.n_cats) pdb.pm() ``` ``` > .../numpy/core/fromnumeric.py(86)_wrapreduction() -> return ufunc.reduce(obj, axis, dtype, out, **passkwargs) (Pdb) ``` That's deep inside NumPy — not code you wrote, and not somewhere you can usefully inspect variables. `u` ("up") walks back out through the call stack toward the frame you did write: ``` (Pdb) u > .../run_no_break.py(10)fit() -> model = statsmodels.api.OLS(sub['y'], statsmodels.api.add_constant(sub['x'])) (Pdb) p i 29 (Pdb) p sub Empty DataFrame Columns: [y, x, cats] Index: [] ``` The 29th stratum has no observations at all — that's the actual bug, and it took two commands to find once positioned at the right frame. Useful `pdb` commands: | Command | Effect | | --- | --- | | `h` / `help` | list all commands | | `l` / `list` | show code around the current line | | `n` / `next` | run the current line | | `s` / `step` | step into the function called on the current line | | `c` / `continue` | run until the next breakpoint | | `unt` / `until` | run until the next line (or a given line number) — useful to finish a loop | | `r` / `run` | run to the end of the current function | | `p` / `print` | print a variable or expression | | `b` / `break` | set a breakpoint; `tbreak` for a one-time breakpoint | | `where` | show the call stack | | `u` / `up`, `d` / `down` | move up or down the call stack | | `q` | quit the debugger | | `` | repeat the previous command | You can also invoke `pdb` on a function directly with `pdb.run("run.fit(run.data, run.n_cats)")` (then type `s` immediately to step into it), or on an entire module with `python -m pdb file.py`, setting breakpoints by line number (`b 9`) or by function name (`b fit`) once inside. ### Common causes of bugs Some Python-specific, some universal: mismatched parentheses; `=` where `==` was meant; comparing floating-point numbers exactly with `==`, which is unsafe because they are only represented to finite precision (`1/3 == 4*(4/12 - 3/12)` is `False`); expecting a scalar and getting an array; silent type conversion happening (or not happening) where you didn't expect it; a typo in a function or variable name; positional arguments passed in the wrong order; and forgetting to define a variable inside a function, so Python's lexical scoping quietly resolves it to a global of the same name from an enclosing scope — which can work fine while you're developing (because the global happens to exist) and then break on a fresh restart. Python also silently drops array dimensions that become extraneous (e.g. indexing a single row out of a 2-D array returns a 1-D array), which can confuse code downstream that expected the original shape. ### Tips for avoiding bugs and catching errors **Defensive programming**, made concrete: check inputs and outputs, use sensible defaults, and fail loudly and specifically. ```python import warnings def mysqrt(x): if isinstance(x, str): raise TypeError(f"What is the square root of '{x}'?") if isinstance(x, (float, int)): if x < 0: warnings.warn("Input value is negative.", UserWarning) return float('nan') # avoid a complex result else: return x**0.5 else: raise ValueError(f"Cannot take the square root of {x}") ``` **Catch a run-time failure and continue**, rather than letting one bad case abort the whole run — the stratified-regression example again, now with the failure handled instead of debugged: ```python params = np.full((n_cats, 2), np.nan) for i in range(n_cats): sub = data[data['cats'] == i] try: model = statsmodels.api.OLS(sub['y'], statsmodels.api.add_constant(sub['x'])) fit = model.fit() params[i, :] = fit.params.values except Exception as error: print(f"Regression cannot be fit for stratum {i}.") ``` Stratum 7 (with no observations) fails and is skipped; the other 29 strata still get fit. A check on sample size beforehand would have caught this particular case, but in general you won't always be able to anticipate every way a call might fail. **Maintain dimensionality.** A row pulled out of a 2-D array silently becomes 1-D, which changes what `axis=0` means to a subsequent call: ```python mat = np.array([[1, 2], [3, 4]]) np.sum(mat, axis=0) # sums columns, as intended mat2 = mat[1, :] np.sum(mat2, axis=0) # sums the elements instead — mat2 is now 1-D if len(mat2.shape) != 2: mat2 = mat2.reshape(1, -1) np.sum(mat2, axis=0) # back to summing columns ``` **Find and avoid global variables.** Code that depends on a variable it didn't create or receive as an argument breaks silently if that global changes. One check: delete the suspect object and see whether the function you're testing still runs. ```python del x # mimic a fresh session, knowing x was global def f(z): y = 3 print(x + y + z) try: f(2) except Exception as error: print(error) ``` **Miscellaneous habits that prevent bugs before they happen**: prefer existing, well-tested library functionality over rewriting it (a standard numerical package will be more efficient and more correct than a first attempt at the same thing); keep code modular so you never have to debug the same logic twice; get a version that is *correct* before making it *fast* — write the naive version first (even a plain loop), then optimise and check the two agree; plan for edge cases in advance rather than patching them in as they appear; write tests early rather than at the end; build up complex code in small, individually-tested steps; make sure the conditions in `if`, `while` and the ranges in `for` are actually robust to the cases you'll hit; and don't hard-code numbers that appear more than once, since a value that needs to change in two places and only gets changed in one is a bug waiting to happen. Finally, **have someone else review your code** where you can — a second reader catches classes of mistake the author is structurally unable to see in their own work. ## Tips for running long analyses Two habits that cost little and save a lot of time on anything that takes more than a few minutes to run: save output at intermediate steps (including the state of the random seed), so a failure partway through — a crash, a dead machine — doesn't mean starting over (`pickle.dump()` is a convenient way to do this); and run the full pipeline on a small subset of the problem first, to check that it works end to end and saves what it should, before committing hours or days of compute to it. ## Reproducible research Interest in reproducibility has grown alongside the complexity of research projects, thin descriptions of methods in published papers, repeated failures to replicate published findings, and outright fraud. Two related but distinct ideas are worth keeping separate: - **Reproducibility**: a second person (or you, later) gets *exactly* the same results from the same data, methods and code. This is harder to achieve than it sounds, and gets harder as time passes, software versions drift, and hardware changes. - **Replicability**: a second study, using new data, obtains results *consistent with* the original when answering the same scientific question. *Provenance* — being able to trace every step of an analysis back to its origin — is the thread that runs through both. Version control (git), scripting (rather than manual, unrecorded steps in an interactive session), and literate-programming documents (Quarto, Jupyter notebooks, which interleave code, output and prose) are the basic tools that make provenance possible. An open question worth sitting with: what, precisely, does something have to satisfy to count as reproducible, or as replicable — and what makes each of those hard in practice? ### Basic strategies - Give each project a directory with meaningful, standardised subdirectories — `code`, `data`, `paper` — rather than a flat pile of files. (The Journal of the American Statistical Association's [template repository](https://github.com/jasa-acs/repro-template) is one worked example of this layout.) - Separate the code for pre-processing, analysis, and figure/table production into different files, named so the pipeline order is obvious — `1-prep.py`, `2-analysis.py`, `3-figs.py`. Pre-processing is often slow; save its output to a data file the analysis script reads in, rather than re-running it every time. The figure-producing script should generate the exact figures that appear in the manuscript, reading from a single saved file (a pickle, say) of everything the figures need, so that "reproduce the figures" and "reproduce the analysis" are cleanly separated steps. - Keep a lab book: a plain-text, dated record of what you did, where the data came from and when, what pre-processing was applied, what each code file is for, and a version number and changelog for the data itself. Where possible, express every change to the data as code applied to a fixed baseline, rather than as an edit you made once and don't have a record of. - Record the versions of everything the code depends on: operating system, language version, and package versions. `pip list` / `conda list` show what's installed; `pip freeze > requirements.txt` and `conda env export > env.yml` capture a recipe that `pip install -r requirements.txt` or `conda env create -f env.yml` can later rebuild (recipes captured this way can be operating-system-specific, but recording versions is worth doing regardless). ### Formal tools - **Literate programming**: do the whole workflow inside a Quarto document or Jupyter notebook, so code, output and narrative stay together. - **Workflow managers**: tools like `make` (built for compiling code, but reusable for any pipeline with dependencies between steps) or Drake track which outputs are stale given which inputs changed, and rerun only what's necessary. - **Package the project itself**, structuring the workflow as an installable Python (or R) package. - **Manage the environment**: Conda environments or virtualenvs for Python; `renv` or `packrat` for R (R's `checkpoint` package, which relied on CRAN snapshots, stopped being viable after those snapshots ended in January 2023 — a reminder that "reproducible" tooling itself needs maintaining). R also has a `config` package for keeping the settings that vary between runs of a workflow — e.g. different input datasets or model settings — in one place, rather than scattered through the code. - **Containers**, most commonly Docker, package not just the language's packages but the whole software environment, so a collaborator (or a service like GitHub Actions or [Binder] (https://mybinder.org)) can run your project inside an environment guaranteed to match yours. Conda can play a similar role for many non-Python dependencies, and is often the lighter-weight option. ## Sources - fall-2025 STAT243, unit 4 ("Good practices"), used as the primary source throughout: `01-overview`, `02-1-good-coding-practices` (editors, style, linting, exceptions/assertions/testing, version control, AI-assisted tools), `03-2-debugging-and-recommendations-for-avoiding-bugs` (debugging strategies, `pdb`, common bugs, tips for avoiding them, tips for running analyses), and `04-4-reproducible-research` (provenance/reproducibility/replicability, basic strategies, formal tools). - fall-2024 STAT243, the same three files, cross-checked against fall-2025: content is essentially identical; fall-2025 adds the AI-assisted-coding-tools section, the `ruff` linting example, and minor polish, so it was preferred wherever the two differed. - stat243-fall-2021, `01-1-good-coding-practices` and `02-4-reproducible-research`: the same unit taught in R rather than Python (the course has since switched languages), reconstructed by a model from a PDF with no text layer and marked accordingly in the source — checked for anything not already covered by the Python versions. Used only for the cross-language asides (R's `assertthat`/`checkmate`/`testthat` packages, and the `config` package for run configuration); the rest duplicates the Python material. - The fall-2026 offering restructured this unit slot into a much larger and differently-scoped unit, "Programming concepts" (text processing and regex, reading and writing data, OS interaction, modules and packages, types and data structures, OOP, functional programming, memory) — a different topic from good coding practices, debugging and reproducibility, and not covered by this chapter. - Referenced but not supplied as course material, and not reproduced here beyond the pointers the lecture itself gives: the PEP 8 style guide, Murrell's *Introduction to Data Technologies* ch. 2, *Journal of Statistical Software* vol. 42 ("19 Ways of Looking at Statistical Software"), Wilson et al., "Best practices for scientific computing" (arXiv:1210.0530), the Gentzkow and Shapiro tutorial for social scientists, the Millman and Perez article on reproducible research, and ch. 11 of *Transparent and Reproducible Social Science Research*.
